title: The siddur
hook: the prayer book, named "order", the most-used Jewish book after the Torah

segments.voice: Yesterday, the circle: the Torah's last letter and its first, together spelling heart. Your line was the end touches the beginning. What did you finish, and start? Today, a new book. Day five hundred thirty-eight.

Walk into almost any synagogue, anywhere in the world, and somewhere near the door you'll find a shelf of matching books, often worn soft at the corners. Some pages carry a wine stain from a holiday, some a child's pencil mark, some the crease of a hand that held them for fifty years. People take one without thinking. It isn't the Torah scroll. For many Jews it's the book they hold more often than any other. For the next stretch of this year, we'll walk through it, in order.
screen: `A SHELF BY THE DOOR.` → `WORN SOFT AT THE CORNERS.` → `THE BOOK HELD MOST OFTEN.`

segments.voice: The word is siddur. It comes from seder, order, the same root as the Passover seder, the ordered meal. A siddur is the prayer book: the weekday prayers, the Sabbath and festival prayers, blessings for food and for waking up, all arranged in the order they're said. That order is the point. Jewish prayer isn't mostly a blank page. It has a shape: blessings, then psalms, then the Shema, then the standing prayer, then the closing. The Talmud discusses many of these prayers centuries before anyone bound them into one volume. The earliest siddurim we know of were written by the geonim, the heads of the great academies in Babylonia: the order of prayer of Rav Amram Gaon in the ninth century, and the siddur of Rav Saadia Gaon in the tenth. Since then, many versions have grown. Ashkenazi Jews, from Central and Eastern Europe, have their rite. Sephardi and Mizrahi Jews, from Spain, North Africa and the Middle East, have theirs. Yemenite communities, Hasidic communities and the modern movements each have siddurim of their own. The core is shared; the details differ, and each community treasures its own. Why give prayer an order at all? One answer: on the days you have no words, the siddur has them. On the days you have too many, it gives them a path. Starting tomorrow, we'll open it, step by step.
screen: `SIDDUR, FROM SEDER: ORDER.` · `PRAYER WITH A SHAPE.` · `AMRAM GAON AND SAADIA GAON.` · `MANY RITES, ONE CORE.` · then, large: `PRAYER HAS AN ORDER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold or open a siddur. If you have one, take it off the shelf and simply hold it. Feel its weight. Open it anywhere and read one line, in Hebrew or in translation. If you don't have one, hold any book you've gone back to many times, and notice why you keep returning. Think of the words people have prayed, in order, for centuries, in many lands, from books like this. The bell holds the time.
Siddur. Order. The Jewish prayer book: the daily prayers, arranged in the order they're said.
Your line: prayer has an order. Today, notice the order of one part of your day, your morning or your evening, and see what shape it already has. Day five hundred thirty-eight.

howItsDone: Jews who pray daily use a siddur for the morning, afternoon and evening services, and a related book, the machzor, for the High Holy Days. Different communities follow different rites (nusach), such as Ashkenaz, Sefard and Edot HaMizrach.
